title: Why Modak Became Lord Ganesha's Favourite Sweet, According to Mythology
excerpt: From a divine contest on Mount Kailash to the ritual offering of 21 modaks, the sweet's bond with the elephant-headed god runs through myth, wisdom and devotion.
body:
• Modak is considered Lord Ganesha's favourite sweet, rooted in a popular Hindu myth in which a divine modak went to the wiser of Parvati's two sons.
  • When Parvati challenged Ganesha and Kartikeya to circle the world three times, Ganesha circumambulated his parents instead, declaring them his entire world.
  • Devotees customarily offer 21 modaks as naivedyam during Ganesh Chaturthi, a number associated with harmony, well-being and completeness.
  • The sweet has come to symbolize wisdom, knowledge and devotion rather than mere festivity.

A Divine Contest on Mount Kailash

Among the foods most inseparable from a deity in Hindu tradition, the modak holds a singular place: it is the sweet Lord Ganesha is said to love above all others. According to one of the most widely retold stories, the bond began when the Devas visited Mount Kailash and presented Lord Shiva and Goddess Parvati with a divine modak, believed to bestow great knowledge and wisdom upon whoever consumed it.

Parvati decided the special sweet should go to one of her two sons, Ganesha or Kartikeya, but only after testing which was more deserving. She challenged them to circle the world three times, promising the modak to whoever returned first. Kartikeya set off at once on his peacock, while Ganesha, whose mount is a mouse, chose an entirely different approach: he walked around his parents and told them that, for him, his mother and father were his entire world.

"He walked around his parents and explained that, for him, his mother and father were his entire world."

— The popular retelling, as recounted by NDTV Food

Impressed by his wisdom and devotion, Parvati awarded the divine modak to Ganesha. The tale cemented the sweet's association with the elephant-headed god, and it is retold in homes across India every Ganesh Chaturthi.

What the Sweet Came to Symbolize

The modak's connection to Ganesha runs deeper than festive custom. In the retelling, the sweet was never just food: it was a vessel of knowledge and wisdom, granted to the son whose devotion outshone his brother's speed. Over centuries, the modak itself came to represent those qualities, and devotees treat the offering as an expression of reverence rather than indulgence.

That symbolism shapes how the sweet is made and served. The classic ukadiche modak, with its rice-flour shell and jaggery-coconut filling, is steamed with care and offered first to the deity before anyone at home tastes it.

The Ritual of 21 Modaks

During Ganesh Chaturthi rituals, it is customary to serve 21 modaks as naivedyam to Lord Ganesha. The number 21 holds sacred significance in Hinduism, representing harmony, well-being and completeness. Once the offering is made, the modaks are distributed as prasad among family, friends and the wider community.

While Ganesh Chaturthi in 2026 fell in late August, the story behind the offering is evergreen: each modak carried to the altar recalls the contest on Kailash and the wisdom that won it.

Modak Beyond the Festival

For the Indian diaspora, the modak is as much a marker of cultural memory as a dessert. Families in the United States and elsewhere steam modaks for the festival, buy them from Indian sweet shops, or simply recount the Kailash story to children. However it is served, the sweet remains what the myth made it: a small, hand-shaped emblem of devotion to Lord Ganesha.
